newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS-Good times roll for NZ markets, post-CPI.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Good times roll for NZ markets, post-CPI.

text.p: News that inflation was lower than expected in the September quarter unleashed a flood of buying across New Zealand markets on Tuesday, while politicians went behind closed doors to discuss who would govern.
The Consumer Price Index rose 0.6 percent in the September quarter and 2.4 percent for the year to September, against expectations of a 2.6 percent rise.
The outcome prompted heavy buying in the interest rate markets as dealers anticipated a formal easing of monetary policy by the central Reserve Bank later this year.

The enthusiasm further fuelled a rally in shares, despite the inconclusive result of Saturday's general election. The top-40 index at one point hit 2,318.07, a rise of 2.37 percent and its highest level since February 1994.

"There has been a lot of tension in the market for a number of weeks, for both political and inflation reasons, and it's like a valve that has been released over the last 48 hours," ASB Bank Economist Anthony Byett said.

Political parties were meeting in Wellington for the first time since the election, which left nationalist New Zealand First holding the balance of power between the conservative National Party and Labour.

Markets have taken an upbeat view of the result, largely because the far left Alliance polled poorly. But coalition building is expected to take weeks, possibly months, and analysts have warned the markets may yet lose their patience.
Economists said the CPI was much better than expected, meaning a fundamental change for New Zealand's interest rate structure and bringing forward a possible Reserve Bank easing.

"All it has done has brought forward when an easing would be possible. Instead of thinking now of the March quarter, we can probably be a bit more optimistic that we may get an easing in December," Byett said.
Campbell Stewart, Head of Equities at SBC Warburg, said the CPI was taken very strongly by the share market.
"There has been a pretty fundamental shift in terms of where the bond market has gone," Stewart said.

Shortly before 3 p.m. (0200 GMT), December bank bill futures were up 27 basis points at 90.93, off their peak of 90.96, on heavy volume. Ninety-day bank bill rates fell about 25 basis points to 9.60 percent.
Finance Minister Bill Birch sought to poor cold water on the rally, warning people not to get over excited about a single set of inflation numbers.
But he said the CPI outcome would improve confidence in the Reserve Bank's ability to hit its zero to two percent inflation target over the next 12 months.

New Zealand First and the National Party, which remains as caretaker government, were holding separate meetings on how coalition negotiations should proceed. The Alliance was expected to present a policy paper setting out its minimum conditions for offering support to Labour.

Centre-right National and its allies won 53 seats in Saturday's election against 50 for the two left-wing parties, Labour and the Alliance, leaving New Zealand First with 17 seats and the balance of power.
National and Labour have both said they aim to form a government with NZ First support, and analysts on balance see a Labour-led coalition as the more likely.
